paragraphs: Recognizing something can involve a feeling of familiarity or the recovery of specific details about a previous encounter. This paper focuses on the second process, recollection. It develops a model based largely on hippocampal anatomy and physiology, motivated by evidence connecting that brain structure to recollection and by the difficulty of explaining recollection through a single, undifferentiated memory process.

The model addresses two particular features of recognition memory. First, people rarely report recollecting a studied event for an item they never studied. Second, interference reduces how often recollection occurs, while apparently leaving the accuracy of successfully recollected information intact. These are separate requirements: a model must explain both whether details are recovered and how trustworthy those details are.

The contribution is an account that captures both patterns within a biologically motivated framework. Its significance is the distinction between recollection becoming less available and recollection becoming less accurate. The reported behavior supports treating those outcomes separately when explaining recognition memory.
neurips-1997-a-hippocampal-model-of-reco.tldr: A hippocampal model explains why interference can reduce recollection without reducing the accuracy of what is recollected.

paragraphs: Optic aphasia presents a striking pattern: someone may struggle to name an object they see, yet still demonstrate its use or name it from an auditory cue. The paper asks how a model can produce this selective impairment when the abilities needed for parts of the task appear relatively preserved.

The proposed explanation introduces partial damage to two pathways. One connects visual input to meaning, and the other connects meaning to a spoken name. Showing how to use a visible object relies on the first pathway, while naming from auditory cues can use the second. Naming a visible object requires both, making it vulnerable to their combined impairment.

The model produces a superadditive effect: the combined damage causes a disproportionately severe deficit on the task requiring both pathways. This matters because a highly specific behavioral impairment need not imply damage to a single specialized route. The authors also report explaining other associated phenomena and generating experimental predictions, extending the account beyond the central naming difficulty.
neurips-1997-a-superadditive-impairment-.tldr: Partial damage to two interacting pathways can explain severe visual naming difficulties alongside relatively preserved related abilities.

paragraphs: Clustering proximity data means organizing items using information about how similar or close they are. This paper treats the collection of that information as part of the clustering problem itself. Instead of separating data generation from analysis, its active approach alternates between analyzing available evidence and deciding what additional evidence to obtain.

The sampling strategy uses expected value of information, a decision-theoretic way of judging how useful a possible observation would be. The central idea is to guide data collection by its anticipated contribution to the analysis. This connects clustering to sequential experiment design, where each new measurement can be chosen in light of what previous measurements have revealed.

The authors position this approach as a way to address sparse proximity information in large datasets. They present applications to grouping image textures without supervision and retrieving information from document databases. These applications illustrate the broader contribution: clustering can actively shape the evidence it receives, rather than relying entirely on a fixed collection of similarities.
neurips-1997-active-data-clustering-0028.tldr: Active clustering chooses new proximity measurements according to their expected usefulness while the clustering process is underway.

paragraphs: Flies begin processing visual motion through an array of elementary motion detectors arranged across the visual field. This paper builds a hardware version of a correlation-based model of those detectors. The goal is to turn a model of insect motion processing into a physical circuit that receives light and responds to movement.

The implementation uses analog CMOS circuitry with integrated photoreceptors. It operates continuously in time, responds in real time, and is described as low power. Combining light sensing and motion processing in the circuit makes the biological model an operational device, allowing its responses to visual patterns to be examined directly.

When tested with drifting sinusoidal gratings, the circuit qualitatively resembles insect motion-sensitive neurons in its responses to spatial frequency, temporal frequency, and motion direction. This is evidence of similar response patterns rather than a claim of exact biological equivalence. The authors propose the circuit both for possible engineering uses and as a component for hardware models of more elaborate insect motion integration.
neurips-1997-an-analog-vlsi-model-of-the.tldr: An analog circuit with integrated light sensors reproduces qualitative motion-response properties of insect neurons in real time.

paragraphs: Compressing data for transmission involves two sources of distortion: replacing the original data with a compact representation and corruption during transmission. This paper develops vector quantization methods that account for both. Its starting cost function includes channel noise, so the representation is optimized for what a receiver may recover.

The authors derive soft topographic vector quantization using maximum entropy and an expectation-maximization style procedure. Deterministic annealing gradually changes a temperature parameter, producing transitions in the code-vector representation. The paper analytically relates the critical temperatures and transition modes to the data covariance and the channel's noise-transition matrix.

This framework yields several algorithms, including an annealed version of the self-organizing map called SSOM. On image data transmitted through a noisy binary symmetric channel, SSOM outperforms LBG, which ignores channel noise, and compares favorably with the more computationally demanding STVQ. The findings connect a principled treatment of transmission errors with a less expensive learning procedure that retains strong reported performance.
neurips-1997-an-annealed-self-organizing.tldr: An annealed self-organizing map learns image compression codes that account for channel noise while comparing favorably with a more demanding method.

paragraphs: This paper studies what feedforward neural networks can generate when used as time-series predictors over long periods. It focuses on stationary, non-chaotic behavior and asks how strongly network architecture constrains the eventual sequence, beyond the particular choices of weights. The key object is the attractor: the long-term behavior toward which the generated sequence settles.

For a perceptron, the authors derive a stationary solution for general weights and find that its flow is typically one-dimensional. They also find that the time needed to approach the stationary solution grows linearly with network size. These results connect a simple architecture to both its eventual dynamics and the duration of its transient behavior.

For multilayer networks, the number of hidden units bounds the number and dimensions of possible attractors. More hidden units can support higher-dimensional long-term behavior. The central implication is specific to the studied non-chaotic regime: architecture helps determine the dynamical possibilities available to a predictor, so long-term prediction cannot be understood solely through its fitted weights.
neurips-1997-analytical-study-of-the-int.tldr: In non-chaotic time-series prediction, network architecture constrains the attractors and long-term dynamics a model can generate.

paragraphs: A change in image brightness can have different physical causes. It might come from shading over a three-dimensional surface, or from paint on that surface. This paper investigates how viewers assign such causes to an image, combining measurements of human judgments with a computational model of the same interpretation problem.

Participants evaluated a set of test images and gave fairly consistent judgments about their surface properties. The model considered alternative explanations involving surface relief or paint. It assigned simple prior probabilities to those explanations, then used Bayesian inference to select the interpretation with the greatest probability given the image.

The algorithm's ratings agreed surprisingly well with the participants' average ratings. This suggests that a probabilistic comparison of physical explanations can capture meaningful aspects of surface perception. The important connection is between ambiguity in the image and preferences among its possible causes: a brightness pattern becomes interpretable when evaluated alongside assumptions about which surface explanations are more plausible.
neurips-1997-bayesian-model-of-surface-p.tldr: A Bayesian model using simple priors over paint and surface relief produces image interpretations that agree well with average human judgments.

paragraphs: This study asks which patterns of sound individual neurons in the primary auditory cortex prefer. The researchers recorded neural activity in awake primates and used a new reverse-correlation technique to estimate receptive fields. These descriptions combine sound frequency with time, allowing a neuron's preferred stimulus to include an evolving pattern across multiple frequencies.

The resulting receptive fields often contain several excitatory and inhibitory regions. In plain language, different parts of a sound pattern can promote or suppress a response. This structure reveals selectivity for more than the presence of a single frequency: neurons can respond to boundaries in frequency composition, boundaries in time, and transitions such as changes in frequency.

The neurons also respond strongly and selectively to continuously frequency-modulated sounds, which the authors compare with drifting visual gratings. Together, the findings reveal organized feature processing in auditory cortex with parallels to visual cortex. The methodological contribution is a way to make those preferences visible across both frequency and ongoing time.
neurips-1997-characterizing-neurons-in-t.tldr: Reverse correlation reveals structured auditory cortical preferences for sound patterns spanning frequency and time.

paragraphs: People can distinguish familiar sounds more finely than unfamiliar ones. This paper investigates a related advantage in early auditory processing, asking whether neural responses are suited to the statistical properties of natural sounds. The hypothesis is that the auditory system uses regularities in its sound environment to encode information efficiently.

The researchers compare narrow-band sounds with two kinds of amplitude modulation: one with naturalistic characteristics and one without them. They measure the information rate carried by auditory spike trains in response to each kind. The comparison therefore concerns how much information neural activity transmits under different sound statistics, rather than relying only on whether neurons respond.

Naturalistic modulation significantly increases the transmitted information rate. This supports the interpretation that auditory neural coding is matched to characteristics of natural acoustic scenes. The experiment makes that connection through controlled properties of amplitude modulation: the reported advantage concerns stimuli carrying those properties, providing evidence for statistical matching within early auditory processing.
neurips-1997-coding-of-naturalistic-stim.tldr: Auditory midbrain spike trains transmit more information for sounds with naturalistic amplitude modulation than for the comparison stimuli.

paragraphs: Reading a badly degraded document involves both identifying individual characters and using the surrounding word to interpret uncertain letters. This paper compares human readers with a neural-network reading model to examine those contributions. The experiments vary document degradation while also considering whether the presented strings are words or non-words.

The study examines word frequency and the legality of non-words alongside degradation level. These factors help distinguish recognition of familiar words from responses to other letter combinations. It also considers character segmentation, the separation of a written string into individual characters, as another influence on reading performance.

The main finding separates two abilities that an overall reading score could combine. The computer model uses word context as efficiently as human readers, but is slightly worse at recognizing characters on their own. Thus, the reported difference does not arise from a general failure to benefit from word context. The comparison helps locate the remaining performance gap in the character-recognition component of the task.
neurips-1997-comparison-of-human-and-mac.tldr: A neural reading model benefits from word context as efficiently as humans but performs slightly worse at recognizing individual characters.

paragraphs: Portfolio allocation is a sequence of decisions: an allocation chosen now affects the choices and costs encountered later. This paper revises a Q-learning approach to that problem. Its main simplification is to use one value function across many assets, providing a shared formulation for evaluating allocation decisions.

The revised approach also supports model-free policy iteration, meaning that the decision policy can be improved without requiring an explicit model of the environment. The authors test the algorithm on real data and then examine how risk management can be expressed within a Markov decision problem. This brings investment preferences into the same sequential framework as allocation choices.

The proposed methods support a portfolio-management system operating across multiple periods while accounting for transaction costs, investor risk preferences, and allocation constraints. These considerations matter because a sequence of attractive allocations may still be undesirable when switching costs or restrictions are included. The stated contribution is a simpler learning formulation and a framework for incorporating those practical decision requirements.
neurips-1997-enhancing-q-learning-for-op.tldr: A revised Q-learning formulation uses one value function for multiple assets and supports portfolio decisions with costs, risk preferences, and constraints.

paragraphs: This paper applies Bayesian neural-network classifiers to automatic sleep staging. Two properties motivate the approach: Bayesian inference incorporates regularization, and network outputs can become more variable in regions unsupported by training data. That second behavior can moderate predictions and provide a basis for detecting unusual inputs.

The authors compare a full Bayesian solution obtained with hybrid Monte Carlo against a single maximum a posteriori solution obtained using an evidence approximation. In five-fold cross-validation, the full Bayesian solution does not outperform the single-solution approach. The result makes the comparison concrete for this application: the more extensive Bayesian treatment does not automatically yield better classification performance.

A second experiment examines how both solutions reject classification of movement artifacts. This addresses a different question from ordinary classification accuracy: whether the system can recognize inputs on which it should withhold a classification. Together, the experiments assess Bayesian learning through both its predictive performance and the potential usefulness of its behavior away from familiar training examples.
neurips-1997-experiences-with-bayesian-l.tldr: In automatic sleep staging, full Bayesian neural-network inference did not outperform a single MAP solution in five-fold cross-validation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical framework for decomposing equivalence classes of functions with several variables. The object being factorized is therefore a class of related functions, with an individual representative providing information about that class. The central question is how to uncover a component structure from the mathematical properties of such a representative.

The authors derive an analytic factorization solution using only local geometric structure. This makes the relationship between local information and the larger decomposition the core of the method. They also show that independent component analysis fits inside their framework as a special case, connecting a familiar decomposition problem to a more general mathematical treatment.

Numerical experiments demonstrate the factorization solution, and the paper offers a preliminary connection to decorrelation. That connection is presented as an initial link rather than a completed equivalence. The contribution combines a general formulation with an analytic solution, showing how an established component-analysis problem can be understood within a broader class of factorizations.
neurips-1997-factorizing-multivariate-fu.tldr: A general factorization framework derives an analytic solution from local geometry and includes independent component analysis as a special case.

paragraphs: Representing an image by detected features can greatly reduce the amount of information that must be stored or processed. It can also make the representation less sensitive to small amounts of image noise. This paper addresses the choice of those features, which is often made through informal design decisions rather than an explicit statistical principle.

The proposed foundation is sufficient statistics: summaries that retain the information needed for the statistical problem under consideration. Applied to feature selection, this idea ties the representation to what it must preserve. The emphasis shifts from simply finding a compact description to choosing features with a principled relationship to the information they summarize.

The authors make the proposal concrete through one-dimensional and two-dimensional signal reconstruction problems. Sparse representations emerge naturally within this treatment. The significance is the connection among statistical sufficiency, compact features, and reconstruction: the paper seeks a reason for choosing a feature set, bringing compression and information preservation into the same account.
neurips-1997-features-as-sufficient-stat.tldr: The paper uses sufficient statistics to give feature selection a principled basis, with sparse representations emerging in signal reconstruction.

paragraphs: Knowing how to perform several tasks separately does not immediately tell an agent how to perform them together. Tasks may compete for attention or resources, making their individual solutions incompatible. This paper asks how existing knowledge of separate tasks can help solve the combined decision problem efficiently.

The authors represent each task as a Markov decision process and merge these into a composite process. They introduce a theoretically grounded dynamic programming algorithm for finding an optimal policy for that composite problem. The approach uses information about the individual tasks to support decisions about the entire collection.

A central feature is that merging can happen dynamically: new tasks can be incorporated online while a solution for ongoing tasks is being developed. The paper analyzes the algorithm and illustrates it with a simple merging example. Its significance lies in treating changing workloads as structured combinations of decision problems, so that knowledge of individual tasks remains useful when the set of simultaneous responsibilities changes.
neurips-1997-how-to-dynamically-merge-ma.tldr: A dynamic programming algorithm combines individual task models into an optimal joint policy and can incorporate new tasks online.

paragraphs: A classifier can be learned directly, or it can be derived from a probabilistic model of the data. This paper investigates how the second strategy behaves when its assumptions are wrong. It studies a specific model in which one hidden binary variable governs the target and all observed attributes, which are conditionally independent given that variable.

Within this model, predicting the most likely value of a variable reduces to applying a linear test to the known values. That property makes a controlled comparison possible. The authors fit the probabilistic model using expectation-maximization and a new covariance-based algorithm, then compare them with a version of Winnow that learns a linear classifier directly.

Performance of the model-based approach deteriorates quickly as the data depart from the assumed structure, falling below the directly trained classifier. The finding identifies a concrete fragility: even when a probabilistic model implies a useful linear decision rule, learning the full model can suffer when its stronger assumptions do not match the data.
neurips-1997-linear-concepts-and-hidden-.tldr: A hidden-variable classifier degrades rapidly under model mismatch and falls behind a directly learned linear classifier.

paragraphs: Useful actions often extend over time: grasping an object or traveling somewhere cannot naturally be described as a single immediate transition. This paper addresses how an agent can learn and plan with actions at multiple temporal levels. Its starting point is the difficulty of expressing such higher-level actions through conventional one-step models.

The authors introduce multi-time models within the framework of Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning. They generalize earlier work on temporal abstraction from prediction to actions, control, and planning. This extends the purpose of an abstract model from describing what may happen over time to supporting choices about what an agent should do.

The theoretical justification comes from the models' relationship to Bellman equations, which connect values across decisions. That relationship establishes their suitability for planning and learning. A grid-world planning task illustrates their potential advantages. The contribution is a formal way to reason over extended actions while retaining the mathematical connection between predictive models and decision-making.
neurips-1997-multi-time-models-for-tempo.tldr: Multi-time models extend reinforcement-learning models to temporally extended actions while preserving a theoretical connection to Bellman-based planning.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an agent learns how its environment behaves and uses that model to plan. This paper examines the interaction between those two activities when local trajectory optimizers work with learned nonparametric models. The practical question is how closely a planner should follow a model that is still being learned.

The authors find that strict consistency can be problematic early in learning. A trajectory planner that fully obeys the learned model may struggle to find reasonable plans. This makes the planner's treatment of the model an important design choice, alongside the choice of model-learning algorithm itself.

Planners often do better when they balance agreement with the model against reducing cost or increasing reward, even when the resulting trajectory is not completely model-consistent. The finding concerns planning during learning, when the model is still developing. Its significance is that the planner and learner must be considered together: insisting on perfect adherence to the current model can hinder the search for useful behavior.
neurips-1997-nonparametric-model-based-r.tldr: Early in model-based learning, trajectory planners can perform better by trading strict model consistency against cost or reward.

paragraphs: Some visual-search displays allow a target to be detected through apparently parallel processing, while others produce behavior associated with serial search. This paper explores whether the difference depends on global information available in the internal representation of a scene. It tests that idea using displays made from line orientations.

The model first compresses each display through principal component analysis. A target detector then examines that compressed representation to determine whether a target is present. Targets remain detectable in displays experimentally associated with parallel search, but not in displays associated with serial search. Variance analysis of the representations supplies a numerical criterion separating the two groups.

The model also produces a pattern of response-time slopes resembling an established search surface relating visual similarity to search behavior. This gives a computational formulation of the role of feature similarity. The result links search difficulty to what survives scene compression, offering a proposed neural account of why some displays make a target globally available and others do not.
neurips-1997-on-parallel-versus-serial-p.tldr: A compressed-scene model distinguishes parallel from serial visual-search displays by whether global target information remains detectable.

paragraphs: Estimating motion becomes difficult when a scene contains several moving objects or overlapping surfaces. Pooling measurements can reduce noise, but combining measurements from different motions can obscure the scene's structure. Mixture models address this by assigning different motion components to different objects, although the number of components often has to be specified beforehand.

This paper shows how to estimate that number automatically through maximum likelihood, given an assumed noise level for the video. The authors derive analytical results identifying how many motion models maximize likelihood for a particular sequence and noise level. The assumed noise therefore plays a direct role in determining the preferred organization.

A real video sequence illustrates transitions between different interpretations of the scene. These phase transitions correspond to changes in its perceptual organization, connecting model selection to how measurements are grouped into objects or surfaces. The contribution is a principled way to choose the number of motion components while making explicit the dependence of that choice on noise.
neurips-1997-phase-transitions-and-the-p.tldr: A maximum-likelihood motion model estimates the number of scene components from an assumed noise level, with transitions between different scene organizations.

paragraphs: A neuron does not have the same opportunity to fire immediately after a spike as it does later. This refractory behavior may influence how precisely it responds when the same stimulus is repeated. The paper investigates that relationship by combining probabilistic spike generation with a refractory period in a model neuron.

With realistic refractoriness, the model closely reproduces both the average firing rate and response precision of a retinal ganglion cell. Matching both properties matters because an average response alone does not describe how consistently spikes occur across repetitions. The result connects the neuron's recent firing history with the precision of its stimulus-driven activity.

The model uses a free firing rate, representing the firing tendency that would exist without refractoriness. The authors suggest that this function may describe a spiking neuron's response better than the peri-stimulus time histogram, which summarizes observed firing around a stimulus. This separates the underlying firing tendency from the constraints imposed by previous spikes, giving refractoriness an explicit explanatory role.
neurips-1997-refractoriness-and-neural-p.tldr: A probabilistic neuron model with realistic refractoriness closely matches both the firing rate and response precision of a retinal ganglion cell.

paragraphs: Regression often involves observations whose reliability varies with the input. This paper models that variation explicitly: both the underlying output and the amount of observation noise are unknown functions. The goal is to learn the signal while also estimating where observations are more or less variable.

The method uses one Gaussian process for the noise-free regression function and a second for the noise variance. Its stated assumption is that the noise varies smoothly with the inputs. The authors also account for uncertainty about the parameters governing both processes, rather than treating those parameters as fully known.

Markov chain Monte Carlo is used to sample from the posterior distribution of the noise level. On a synthetic dataset, the inferred noise variance closely approximates the true variance. This demonstrates that the framework can recover changing observation variability in the reported setting. Its significance is the joint treatment of the response and its noise: uncertainty about measurement variability becomes part of the regression problem itself.
neurips-1997-regression-with-input-depen.tldr: Two Gaussian processes jointly model a regression function and smoothly varying noise, recovering the noise variance well on synthetic data.

paragraphs: The S-Map is designed to combine two desirable properties of topographic mapping networks: the capacity to organize itself during learning and a probabilistic interpretation of the resulting model. The paper draws these properties from the Self-Organizing Map and Generative Topographic Mapping, respectively, and brings them together through a simple learning algorithm.

The simulations focus on whether useful organization emerges from a random initial configuration. They suggest that S-Map has a stronger tendency to self-organize than Generative Topographic Mapping. This matters because the starting arrangement is part of the learning problem: an algorithm must develop structure from an initially unorganized configuration.

The authors also simplify the learning procedure further so that it uses pure Hebbian learning. They report that this preserves the network's qualitative behavior. The contribution is therefore both a combined mapping approach and evidence that its characteristic organization can survive a simpler update mechanism. The stated comparison concerns self-organization in simulations, while the simplification concerns preservation of qualitative network behavior.
neurips-1997-s-map-a-network-with-a-simp.tldr: S-Map combines self-organization with probabilistic interpretation and retains its qualitative behavior under a simplified Hebbian learning rule.

paragraphs: Boosting seeks to improve classification by combining learners that need only perform somewhat better than chance. This paper applies AdaBoost to neural networks and examines how to train those networks within the boosting procedure. The focus is on practical training choices for making neural-network classifiers benefit from adaptive boosting.

The authors compare two ways of giving training examples different influence. One changes how the training set is sampled; the other changes the weights in the cost function. Both approaches let the boosting procedure alter which examples matter most, but they introduce that emphasis at different points in network training.

The reported system reaches about 1.4% error on online handwritten digits collected from more than 200 writers. A boosted multilayer network obtains 1.5% error on UCI Letters and 8.1% on the UCI satellite dataset. These results demonstrate the application across several classification tasks. The paper's contribution combines those outcomes with a comparison of mechanisms for connecting adaptive example emphasis to neural-network training.
neurips-1997-training-methods-for-adapti.tldr: The paper compares sampling and cost-weighting methods for boosting neural networks and reports results on handwriting, letter, and satellite classification.

paragraphs: This paper models video traffic as a time series, focusing on dependencies that occur over both short and long intervals. Its central change is the representation used for modeling. Instead of working directly with the sequence in the time domain, the authors construct a model of its wavelet coefficients.

The proposed wavelet model provides a unified treatment of short-range and long-range dependence. These are two aspects of temporal structure that the authors aim to capture simultaneously. The representation therefore serves a modeling purpose: it brings behavior at different temporal ranges into a single framework, rather than addressing only one range of dependence.

The authors also identify computational efficiency in building the model and generating high-quality video traffic as advantages. They state that the model makes performance analysis feasible as well. Together, these claims position the approach as useful for representing traffic, producing modeled traffic sequences, and analyzing performance with the resulting model. The contribution is the connection between the wavelet representation and those modeling tasks.
neurips-1997-wavelet-models-for-video-ti.tldr: Modeling video traffic through wavelet coefficients captures short- and long-range dependence while supporting efficient generation and performance analysis.
